title: Texas Rangers Pursue Criminal Case Over 27 Camp Mystic Flood Deaths
excerpt: Search-warrant affidavits allege camp leadership committed manslaughter and criminally negligent homicide in the July 2025 Guadalupe River flood.
body:
• The Texas Rangers are pursuing a criminal investigation into Camp Mystic, with a judge approving 14 search warrants for the electronic data of the camp's owners and staff.
  • Affidavits allege manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide, injury to a child and deadly conduct in the deaths of 25 campers and two counselors.
  • Investigators say the camp lacked emergency plans and drills and failed to move children from low-lying cabins despite monitoring flood warnings overnight.

The Texas Rangers are pursuing criminal charges against Camp Mystic over the July 4, 2025, flood that killed 27 people at the Christian all-girls camp in Hunt, Texas, according to search-warrant affidavits reported by The New York Times. A Kerr County state district judge approved 14 warrants on Friday seeking the electronic data of the Eastland family, which ran the camp, along with other staff members. No charges have been filed, and a camp representative did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

What the affidavits allege

Texas Ranger Brant C. Johnston wrote that camp leadership committed manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide, injury to a child, abandoning or endangering a child, and deadly conduct. The warrants seek phone data from July 3 through October 17, 2025 — text messages, emails, photos, location information, search history, app data and deleted materials — to establish what camp leadership knew, when they knew it, and what they did in response.

FOX 4 obtained the affidavit for Edward Eastland, a camp director who was on the grounds that night. Johnston wrote that the camp had inadequate emergency plans, failed to conduct emergency drills or training, and in some cabins did not have enough adult counselors. Its owners, he wrote, neglected to relocate children from low-lying cabins despite having monitored late-night flood warnings.

"Camp Mystic, LLC was aware of and consciously disregarded a substantial and unjustifiable risk of death to the campers in their care."

— Brant C. Johnston, Texas Ranger, in the search-warrant affidavit

"Young campers cannot reasonably be expected to independently recognize a rapidly developing, life-threatening hazard or to organize and execute an evacuation absent direction from an adequate number of adult supervisors."

— Brant C. Johnston, Texas Ranger, in the search-warrant affidavit

The night of the flood

Twenty-five campers and two teenage counselors died as the Guadalupe River surged beyond its banks before dawn on July 4, 2025. Camp owner Richard "Dick" Eastland also died in the flood. In all, 119 people died across Kerr County. For decades, Camp Mystic had been a summer institution for generations of Texas families — horseback riding, canoeing, fishing and Bible studies on the Guadalupe River.

The camp had planned to reopen this year for more than 800 girls in areas away from the hardest-hit grounds. But in April it withdrew its application for a license to operate and decided not to reopen. It has since filed for bankruptcy reorganization.

A record of warnings

The affidavits lean heavily on the Texas Legislature committee's final report, which found the camp did not have state-required written emergency plans or adequate evacuation plans. Investigators Casey Garrett and Michael Massengale, hired by the Legislature, described cascading failures in a 115-page report, citing communication lapses between state and local authorities and lackluster evacuation instructions given to counselors.

Edward Eastland testified before the committee earlier this year. In April, he broke down in tears during a court hearing in Austin on a lawsuit against the camp. A separate investigation by ProPublica and the Texas Tribune found that lawmakers repeatedly failed over 60 years to pass flood protections for the state's most flood-prone areas. The Rangers' investigation began in March 2026.

Why this matters for families

Texas is home to one of the largest Indian-American communities in the United States, and thousands of diaspora families entrust their children to summer camps across the state each year. The criminal inquiry — an unusual escalation beyond the civil lawsuits already filed — will set a precedent for how camp operators are held accountable for emergency preparedness. For parents evaluating camps, the case is already reshaping the questions to ask: written emergency plans, drill records, counselor ratios in each cabin, and how flood warnings are monitored overnight.

What's next

Prosecutors will review the electronic evidence before deciding whether to bring charges. The camp's bankruptcy reorganization proceeds in parallel, and civil litigation from victims' families continues. The Legislature's findings are also expected to drive new state requirements for youth camps operating in flood zones.
